title: Stochastic convex bandits: one-point observations with independent Gaussian noise.
summary: A fixed unknown convex function is defined on the unit Euclidean ball. Each round reveals one value with independent Gaussian noise at the point where loss is incurred. The objective is cumulative true function loss. The unknown additive offset is not supplied as free information.

description_paragraphs: A fixed unknown convex function is defined on the unit Euclidean ball. Each round reveals one value with independent Gaussian noise at the point where loss is incurred. The objective is cumulative true function loss. The unknown additive offset is not supplied as free information.

model.instance: The unknown fixed function $f:B_2^d(1)\to\mathbb R$ is continuous, convex, and Euclidean 1-Lipschitz. Each round selects one loss-incurring point $x_t$ and observes $f(x_t)$ plus independent standard Gaussian noise. The additive level $f(0)$ is not public.

bounds.derivation: First use $n_0=\lceil2\log(4T)\rceil$ charged rounds at the origin to estimate $f(0)$ by $\widehat f_0$. With probability at least $1-1/(2T)$, the estimation error is at most one, so $|f(x)-\widehat f_0|\le2$ throughout the unit ball. With smoothing radius $\delta_{\mathrm{sm}}$, choose a center in the contracted ball and query the center plus $\delta_{\mathrm{sm}} u_t$, where $u_t$ is a random unit direction. The loss is incurred at this query point. The estimator $g_t=(d/\delta_{\mathrm{sm}})(Y_t-\widehat f_0)u_t$ has conditional second moment at most $5d^2/\delta_{\mathrm{sm}}^2$. Smoothing and contraction cost $O(\delta_{\mathrm{sm}} T)$, and the online gradient term is $O(d\sqrt T/\delta_{\mathrm{sm}})$. Choose $\delta_{\mathrm{sm}}\asymp\sqrt d\,T^{-1/4}\le1/2$. Under $T\ge C_0d^2$, the initialization cost $O(\log T)$ and the failure-event contribution are absorbed. Each round uses one charged function value; the baseline is not obtained for free.

bounds.derivation: Use the same charged initialization to estimate $\widehat f_0$. Public ball geometry supports the required sampling and membership tests. Retain the source polylogarithmic order without claiming optimal runtime.
